metadata.description:
Case name: Carter v. United States

Opinion filed: 2000-06-12

Docket No.: 99-5716

Citations:
• 147 L. Ed. 2d 203
• 120 S. Ct. 2159
• 530 U.S. 255
• 2000 U.S. LEXIS 3963

Case holding summaries:
• explaining that ―the presumption in favor of scienter demands only that we read (continued…
• explaining that general intent (as opposed to specific intent) requires “that the defendant possessed knowledge [only] with respect to the actus reus of the crime”
• noting that ―Congress could have simply punished ‗robbery‘ or ‗larceny‘ as some States have done . . . thereby leaving the definition of these terms to the common law‖
• concluding that the presumption in favor of scienter only required proof of general intent in federal bank robbery statute that was silent as to the mens rea requirement
• stating that the canons of statutory interpretation require courts to first examine the statutory text
• noting just because the interpretation results in an anomaly, that does not mean it is an absurdity which justifies statute modification
• referring to Jones in determining elements of offense
• "a `cluster of ideas' from the common law should be imported into statutory text only when Congress employs a common-law term. "
• holding that value is an element for purposes of 18 U.S.C. § 2113(b
• noting just because the interpretation results in an anomaly, that does not mean it is an absurdity which justifies statute modification
• explaining that § 2112 "leav[es] the definition of [robbery] to the common law"
• agreeing that the elements test requires more than a mere “textual compari- son” of the statutes in question and applying “normal principles of statutory construction”
• explaining that general intent (as opposed to specific intent) requires “that the defendant possessed knowledge [only] with respect to the actus reus of the crime”
• courts are required to "read into a statute only that mens rea which is necessary to separate wrongful conduct from 'otherwise innocent conduct'" (quoting United States v. X-Citement Video, 513 U.S. 64, 72 (1994))
• "The canon on imputing common-law meaning applies only when Congress makes use of a statutory term with established meaning at common law...." (emphasis in original)
• "The presumption in favor of scienter requires a court to read into a statute only that mens rea which is necessary to separate wrongful conduct from otherwise innocent conduct."
• describing “feloniously” as equivalent to “ ‘intent’ ”
• "The presumption in favor of scienter requires a court to read into a statute only that mens rea which is necessary to separate wrongful conduct from `otherwise innocent conduct.'"
• holding that courts must read a mens rea into a criminal statute only to the extent necessary to distinguish between wrongful and innocent conduct
• noting just because the interpretation results in an anomaly, that does not mean it is an absurdity which justifies statute modification
• “[T]he title of a statute is of use only when it sheds light on some ambiguous word or phrase in the statute itself.” (internal quotation marks and alterations omitted)
• referring to Jones in determining elements of offense
• noting that title of statute may be of use when it sheds light on an ambiguous phrase
• "In analyzing a statute, we begin by examining the text, not by `psychoanalyzing those who enacted it.'"
• distinguishing between general and specific intent requirements
• discussing the federal bank robbery statute, 18 U.S.C. § 2113(a)
• agreeing that the elements test requires more than a mere "textual comparison" of the statutes in question and applying "normal principles of statutory construction"
• "[T]he title of a statute is of use only when it sheds light on some ambiguous word or phrase in the statute itself."
• “[T]he title of a statute is of use only when it sheds light on some ambiguous word or phrase in the statute itself.”
• noting just because the interpretation results in an anomaly, that does not mean it is an absurdity which justifies statute modification
• equating the “specific intent” to steal with the intent to “permanently . . . deprive” the victim of its property
• "In analyzing a statute, we begin by examining the text."
• holding that value is an element for purposes of 18 U.S.C. § 2113(b
• explaining that general intent, as opposed to specific intent, requires “that the defendant possessed knowledge [only] with respect to the actus reus of the crime”
• holding that value is an element for purposes of 18 U.S.C. § 2113(b) because the first paragraph "requires that the property taken have `value exceeding $1,000'" and the second paragraph "refers to property of `value not exceeding $1,000,'" thus "describ[ing][two] distinct offenses"
• noting that sleepwalking would be a defense to 18 U.S.C. S 2113(a) even if it were a general intent crime
• holding that 18 U.S.C. § 2113(a) is not a specific intent crime
• holding that 18 U.S.C. § 2113(a) is not a specific intent crime
• “[Section] 2113(b) requires an element not required by § 2113(a) -- three in fact -- and therefore is not a lesser included offense of § 2113(a).”
• Bank larceny [18 U.S.C. § 2113(b)] is not a lesser included offense of robbery [18 U.S.C. § 2113(c)]
• noting that "all agree" that the adverb "feloniously," which modified the term"takes" in a version of 18 U.S.C. S 2113(a) enacted in 1934, "is equivalent to `intent to steal'"
• resort to statutory titles is permissible to address statutory ambiguities
• "The presumption in favor of scienter requires a court to read into a statute only that mens rea which is necessary to separate wrongful conduct from `otherwise innocent conduct.'"
• declining heightened mens rea under 18 U.S.C. § 2113(a) because “forceful taking—even by a defendant who takes under a good-faith claim of right—falls outside the realm of . . . ‘otherwise innocent’ [conduct]”
• noting just because the interpretation results in an anomaly, that does not mean it is an absurdity which justifies statute modification
• explaining that knowingly engaging in acts of using force and taking money satisfies “general intent” requirement of bank robbery, even if defendant might not intend to deprive bank permanently of possession of money
